Flamingo Rescue

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
People from all walks of life stand together to save hundreds of lessor flamingo chicks.

Unique Selling Point:
Community organisations, the SPCA in Kimberley, conservationists and private individuals are standing together to rescue more then 1000 lesser flamingo chicks are dying in the scorching heat just outside Kimberley. Volunteers from the community of Kimberley have been collecting newly hatched chicks from their abandoned nests and taking them to the local SPCA where they are hydrated, fed and looked after a local vet. Some 900 chicks were flown to Wonderboom Airport where they are being taken care of by Mike Bolhuis on his private property. The rest of the chicks are said to go to various wildlife rehabilitation centres across the country. Experts say if the rain stays away the pan could be completely dry within 2 to 4 weeks, forcing the adult flamingoes to move away.

Summary:
The Kamfers Dam outside Kimberley is drying up fast. It is home to approximately 60,000 lesser flamingoes and they have been breeding at the dam for about 30 years. The dam is one of only four breeding sites for the lesser flamingo in the world. But disaster has struck. A vast area where the flamingoes have nested has dried out completely, leaving nests exposed. During the hot days the flamingoes leave their nests to move to the the small area that still has water leaving the chicks and eggs exposed. Eggs are breeding out and the chicks are vulnerable. In some instances the chicks are so dehydrated from the heat that they are unable to hatch themselves. Now the community of Kimberley have come together and have collected about 3,000 chicks so far. They are being cared for at the Kimberley SPCA, and flown to various rehab centres across the country. So far, about 1,400 chicks are at Mike Bolhuis' farm just north of pretoria, where he has hired experts to help look after the chicks.

Further information:
There are various factors contributing to the dramatic drop in water levels at Kamfers dam -- The biggest issue is the fact that the Homevale sewage treatment plant is not functional. The treatment facility is supposed to treat Kimberley and the surrounding township's effluent water, treat it and then release the treated water into Kamfers Dam. That water is then used by the local golf course and the local mine, Ekapa Minerals - the remaining water is then available to the flamingoes in the dam. However, there is virtually no water flowing into the dam from Homevale, because the plant is not functioning. Instead about 10 megalitres of raw effluent flows into a nearby wetland and veld on a daily basis. Locals say this is 90% of the problem. On top of that the mine is still pumping water from the dam - because they have to and have the licences to do so - and on top of it the area has had no rain for over a year.

There is a lot of internal politics around Kamfers Dam. The property belongs to Herbert and Brenda Booth, thus it is not a formally protected conservancy, which make conservationists reluctant to get involved. Mike Bolhuis, the detective and philanthropist has made his property outside Pretoria available to rear and rehabilitate some 1,500 chicks rescued from the dried up pan. Ekapa Mining have made their private jet available to fly the rescued chicks all over the country. (including to Pretoria). The community of Kimberley have been amazing. At the local SPCA are about 100 cars parked, with hundreds of volunteers assisting to feed chicks, collect chicks from the dam. They're building temporary enclosures to keep the chicks safe. There are even two locals vets assisting with the weak and sick ones. The chicks are fed a special concoction, via syringe and it's amazing to see how quickly they grow and become strong.

The question is what is to become of the flamingoes once they are grown-up. Will they be returned to Kamfers, or end up somewhere else. Mike Bolhuis is determined that his 1,500 chicks will be rehabilitated back to the wild.

Additional controversy lies in the fact that: Some conservationists are questioning the way in which this mass operation is handled. There are questions around Mike Bolhuis' permits and their legitimacy. And there are even allegations that Mike Bolhuis is involved in wildlife trafficking, and that the flamingoes are destined to end up at luxury estates in the Middle East.

But, ignoring the politics, it is a story of people of all walks of life coming together and saving thousands of chicks that faced certain death.

Press Release:


Flamingo Rescue
In a heart-rending show of compassion and solidarity, people from all walks of life have come together to save what is left of thousands of flamingo eggs and chicks at Kamfers Dam outside Kimberley. Carte Blanche unpacks the perfect storm of soaring summer temperatures, crippling drought and failing municipal sewage infrastructure that caused the ecological disaster that has seen flamingo eggs dry out and chicks abandoned on their nests.
Producer: Stenette Grosskopf
Presenter: Claire Mawisa
Watch the trailer


Script:


FLAMINGO RESCUE




V/O
At first glance, all looks well at Kamfers Dam outside Kimberley in the Northern Cape, but as you get closer the large groups of flamingos huddling in the shallow receded puddles and the rows and rows of abandoned nests on the shoreline are clear signs that all is not well here...
LINK
Kamfers Dam is home to about 50,000 lesser flamingos and is one of only four breeding sites in Africa.

Kamfers Dam has all but dried up and not just because of a lack of rain – it's a perfect storm of; long-term municipal difficulties, soaring summer temperatures, water use demands and prolonged drought, --- This has lead to the pan drying up to such an extent, that many flamingos abandoned their nests,… and newly hatched chicks were left to fend for themselves.
Herbert & Brenda Booth
Herbert: You cannot believe it. You walk around and you see these poor little chicks running around and the eggs that are just deserted. It is heartbreaking.

Brenda: And they hatch only to die....
V/O
Landowners, Herbert and Brenda Booth raised the alarm and within hours people from all over South Africa sprang into action.
Linja Allen
Die gemeenskap het hulle harte ongelooflik oopgemaak teenoor hierdie projek. Oral is vrywilligers wat help.
V/O
Linja Allen, chairperson of the community organisation, Saam Staan Kimberley has been coordinating the rescue efforts at the dam. For days, volunteers scoured the pan, rounding up abandoned and weak chicks, and transporting them to the SPCA in Kimberley.
Linja Allen
Daar's die heeltyd konstant mense in en uit by the SPCA. Mense bring donasies, mense bring verwarmingsligte, komberse, plekke bring vir ons kos om te eet deur die dag soos ons beweeg.
V/O
The local SPCA has been bustling for almost 2 weeks now. Initially temporary enclosures were erected to house the stronger chicks, and while some people were feeding,… others were helping the little ones to take a bath.
Mario vd Westhuizen
Hier is omtrent so 1,200 tot 1,500 kuikens op hierdie stadium wat ons almal moet bymekaarkry en help en voer en alles.
V/O
Mario van der Westhuizen heads up the Kimberley SPCA and he's pleased with their efforts despite a few mortalities.
Mario vd Westhuizen
Dit gaan baie goed, ons het baie min verloor deur die nag. Ons het 'n klomp in die clinic wat die veeartse na kyk, ons het spanne oralste, veeartse is hierso, mense wat kennis het wat vir ons help en alles, so ja, dit gaan baie baie goed op die stadium.
V/O
Security specialist and well-known investigator, Mike Bolhuis has long had his own flock of flamingos. From the outset he opened his heart to the destitute chicks.
Mike Bolhuis
Last Thursday when I heard of this I immediately took action. I jumped the red tape and the legislations and everything else, got them on a plane and flew them here.
V/O
About 900 chicks were flown to Pretoria and are currently cared for at his estate north of the city.
Mike Bolhuis
These chicks are very very frail. First of all they've been in the sun, they've been dehydrated and they were in a very bad state. So, I got the best doctors involved, the best animal lovers, the authorities, obviously as well. And we started rehydrating them and feeding them.
V/O
Vetrinarian Robert Cambell is working closely with Bolhuis to ensure the chicks receive optimal care.
Campbell
Out of these we might still lose one or two percent. The reason being some of these might be getting pecked by another one, because like in nature they have competition for survival of the fittest and they've got to learn to bath. Some of them don't know, they fall asleep in the water. That's why we have somebody literally monitoring them here.


V/O
Here too, volunteers are working around the clock to feed and care for the chicks.
Volunteer
Claire: I'm so worried that they look so delicate.

Ja, they were I the beginning but they're so strong now.
V/O
Although he has been receiving some donations from the public, this project has largely been funded by Bolhuis himself.
Mike Bolhuis
Claire: And why is this so important to you?

Well I see this case not only as a animal lover but as a crime. This is because of human neglect. The city council there, the authorities, the municipality, the mines... They are all guilty.
LINK
This is what a flamingo nest looks like and normally there'd be water halfway up the nest and the flamingos would be around the eggs. But because there's no water the flamingos are way over there and so when these eggs hatch the chicks are left vulnerable.
V/O
Kamfers Dam gets most of it's water from the Homevale Waste Water Treatment Plant, but a portion of the waste water is used by the local mine.
Jahn Hohne
We've been tracking the levels of the water in the Kamfers Dam for the past 12 months and continually raising alerts that the inflow of water is not matching the outflow and our pumping requirements from Kamfers Dam.
V/O
CEO of Ekapa Mining, Jahn Hohne, is also a birdlover and has sponsored the aircraft used to airlift chicks from the SPCA in Kimberley to various destinations across the country. While some people point fingers at the mine for extracting water from the dam, Hohne joins the chorus of voices that lay the blame squarely at the feet of the local municipality.
Jahn Hohne
The situation immediately is as a result of way too little effluent sewage coming to Homevale treatment works and the bulk by 80 to 90% of the sewage of kimberley is currently flowing freely into the neighbouring property of Platfontein.


V/O
CEO of Birdlife South Africa, Mark Anderson has a long history with the lesser flamingos of Kamfers Dam. He says the ongoing drought in the Northern Cape is also a factor to consider.
Mark Anderson
Kimberley has experienced a really hot summer – very little rain, high evaporation rates, and that's contributed to the problem, but largely there's been much less water flowing in from the Homevale waste water treatment works.
V/O
Sello Matsie, spokesperson for the Sol Plaatjie Municipality is quick to point out that the treated waste water is supplied to Kamfers for free and is not a given right...
Sello Matsie
That pan on its own is a private property. It's not a government.... We have no contractual obligation to supply.
Mark Anderson
I disagree, the municipality has an integrated development plan and a spacial development framework – in those documents they recognise Kamfers Dam as a conservancy and hence it needs to be protected and in order to promote the presence of flamingos at Kamfers Dam you need water. ….. To the city and the municipality.
V/O
Matsie does concede that the city has problems with infrastructure. One of the major pump stations known as Gogga, that moves sewage to Homevale Treatment plant, has been out of order 5 times already in the month of January alone – due to cable theft. And that's just the beginning...
Sello Matsie
The line between here from Gogga pump station, to Homevale has caved in, in multiple areas.And the reason for that s that the methane gas inside the pipeline has corroded the concrete structure.
V/O
And since the sewage cannot be pumped to Homevale, it simply runs into the Platfontein wetland on the North-Western side of the city... Resident and avid birder, Brian Culver says he first reported this ongoing sewage spillage in 2014.
Brian Culver
This is 90% of the reason why we are having the problems at Kamfers Dam with the chicks at the moment. Every drop you see here now is supposed to be going into Kamfers. There is no stormwater stuff here because it's not raining.
V/O
Matsie says the municipality is pro-active, it is repairing the caved-in pipeline and even building a new additional line that will be completed later this year.
Sello Matsie
What we want to dispel, despite these challenges having started – even if it's four years ago – that we just folded our arms and did nothing.

Claire: It took 4 years to solve a problem or more. That's where people's frustrations come in...

The four years must take into account. Because I'm a resident. I was born here. This infrastructure that you're talking of didn't even include me. And this population here is 80% of the entire city.
V/O
According to Matsie the original infrastructure was meant to service a small portion of the community and keeping up with the growing demand is a challenge..., and while thousands of litres of water run into a veld, with sewage contaminating the landscape, the eggs on the dam continue to hatch …
V/O
To date they have rescued about 3,000 chicks and almost all of them have been relocated to different rehabilitation centres across the country.
Linja Allen
Claire: Is the ultimate goal to release them back?

Ja. We really want to put them back into nature.
Mike Bolhuis
Claire: Are there guarantees that these chicks will be re-released into the wild? So how transparent is this process going to be?

I'm saying in emphatically I will not tolerate that these animals will be left behind or neglected. And I will make sure that the authorities and the people that are the experts, that their will and wishes, happen.
V/O
But there is still a long road ahead.

Rehabilitators need to try and mitigate the risks of disease and the possibility that the chicks will become too familiar with humans, ...and Kamfers Dam needs to be restored to the prime flamingo neighbourhood it once was...




PROMO 10”
A potential ecological disaster at Kimberley has lead to a massive flamingo rescue operation, but will the birds find their way home again?
PROMO 15”
The drying up of Kamfers Dam in Kimberley has resulted in thousands of lesser flamingo chicks in need of rescue...

UPSOUND: MIKE BOLHUIS
When I heard of this I immediately took action. I jumped the red tape and the legislations and everything else, got them on a plane and flew them here.
PROMO 15”
Thousands of flamingo chicks have been rescued from Kamfers Dam in Kimberley where they were faced with certain death.

UPSOUND: MIKE BOLHUIS
These chicks are very very frail. First of all they've been in the sun, they've been dehydrated and they were in a very bad state.

PROMO 30”
In the scorching Kimberley heat thousands of abandoned lesser flamingo chicks faced certain death.

UPSOUND HERBERT & BRENDA BOOTH
Herbert: You cannot believe it. You walk around and you see these poor little chicks running around and the eggs that are just deserted. It is heartbreaking.


But South Africans have come together and launched a massive rescue operation, collecting about 3,000 chicks and distributing them to rehabilitation facilities across the country.

UPSOUND MIKE BOLHUIS
When I heard of this I immediately took action. I jumped the red tape and the legislations and everything else, got them on a plane and flew them here.

Mike Bolhuis Claire: And why is this so important to you? Well I see this case not only as a animal lover but as a crime. This is because of human neglect. The city council there, the authorities, the municipality, the mines... They are all guilty. LINK This is what a flamingo nest looks like and normally there'd be water halfway up the nest and the flamingos would be around the eggs. But because there's no water the flamingos are way over there and so when these eggs hatch the chicks are left vulnerable. V/O Kamfers Dam gets most of it's water from the Homevale Waste Water Treatment Plant, but a portion of the waste water is used by the local mine. Jahn Hohne We've been tracking the levels of the water in the Kamfers Dam for the past 12 months and continually raising alerts that the inflow of water is not matching the outflow and our pumping requirements from Kamfers Dam. V/O CEO of Ekapa Mining, Jahn Hohne, is also a birdlover and has sponsored the aircraft used to airlift chicks from the SPCA in Kimberley to various destinations across the country. While some people point fingers at the mine for extracting water from the dam, Hohne joins the chorus of voices that lay the blame squarely at the feet of the local municipality. Jahn Hohne The situation immediately is as a result of way too little effluent sewage coming to Homevale treatment works and the bulk by 80 to 90% of the sewage of kimberley is currently flowing freely into the neighbouring property of Platfontein. V/O CEO of Birdlife South Africa, Mark Anderson has a long history with the lesser flamingos of Kamfers Dam. He says the ongoing drought in the Northern Cape is also a factor to consider. Mark Anderson Kimberley has experienced a really hot summer – very little rain, high evaporation rates, and that's contributed to the problem, but largely there's been much less water flowing in from the Homevale waste water treatment works. V/O Sello Matsie, spokesperson for the Sol Plaatjie Municipality is quick to point out that the treated waste water is supplied to Kamfers for free and is not a given right... Sello Matsie That pan on its own is a private property. It's not a government.... We have no contractual obligation to supply. Mark Anderson I disagree, the municipality has an integrated development plan and a spacial development framework – in those documents they recognise Kamfers Dam as a conservancy and hence it needs to be protected and in order to promote the presence of flamingos at Kamfers Dam you need water. ….. To the city and the municipality. V/O Matsie does concede that the city has problems with infrastructure. One of the major pump stations known as Gogga, that moves sewage to Homevale Treatment plant, has been out of order 5 times already in the month of January alone – due to cable theft. And that's just the beginning... Sello Matsie The line between here from Gogga pump station, to Homevale has caved in, in multiple areas.And the reason for that s that the methane gas inside the pipeline has corroded the concrete structure. V/O And since the sewage cannot be pumped to Homevale, it simply runs into the Platfontein wetland on the North-Western side of the city... Resident and avid birder, Brian Culver says he first reported this ongoing sewage spillage in 2014. Brian Culver This is 90% of the reason why we are having the problems at Kamfers Dam with the chicks at the moment. Every drop you see here now is supposed to be going into Kamfers. There is no stormwater stuff here because it's not raining. V/O Matsie says the municipality is pro-active, it is repairing the caved-in pipeline and even building a new additional line that will be completed later this year. Sello Matsie What we want to dispel, despite these challenges having started – even if it's four years ago – that we just folded our arms and did nothing. Claire: It took 4 years to solve a problem or more. That's where people's frustrations come in... The four years must take into account. Because I'm a resident. I was born here. This infrastructure that you're talking of didn't even include me. And this population here is 80% of the entire city. V/O According to Matsie the original infrastructure was meant to service a small portion of the community and keeping up with the growing demand is a challenge..., and while thousands of litres of water run into a veld, with sewage contaminating the landscape, the eggs on the dam continue to hatch … V/O To date they have rescued about 3,000 chicks and almost all of them have been relocated to different rehabilitation centres across the country. Linja Allen Claire: Is the ultimate goal to release them back? Ja. We really want to put them back into nature. Mike Bolhuis Claire: Are there guarantees that these chicks will be re-released into the wild? So how transparent is this process going to be? I'm saying in emphatically I will not tolerate that these animals will be left behind or neglected. And I will make sure that the authorities and the people that are the experts, that their will and wishes, happen. V/O But there is still a long road ahead. Rehabilitators need to try and mitigate the risks of disease and the possibility that the chicks will become too familiar with humans, ...and Kamfers Dam needs to be restored to the prime flamingo neighbourhood it once was... PROMO 10” A potential ecological disaster at Kimberley has lead to a massive flamingo rescue operation, but will the birds find their way home again? PROMO 15” The drying up of Kamfers Dam in Kimberley has resulted in thousands of lesser flamingo chicks in need of rescue... UPSOUND: MIKE BOLHUIS When I heard of this I immediately took action. I jumped the red tape and the legislations and everything else, got them on a plane and flew them here. PROMO 15” Thousands of flamingo chicks have been rescued from Kamfers Dam in Kimberley where they were faced with certain death. UPSOUND: MIKE BOLHUIS These chicks are very very frail. First of all they've been in the sun, they've been dehydrated and they were in a very bad state. PROMO 30” In the scorching Kimberley heat thousands of abandoned lesser flamingo chicks faced certain death. UPSOUND HERBERT & BRENDA BOOTH Herbert: You cannot believe it. You walk around and you see these poor little chicks running around and the eggs that are just deserted. It is heartbreaking. But South Africans have come together and launched a massive rescue operation, collecting about 3,000 chicks and distributing them to rehabilitation facilities across the country. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): People from all walks of life stand together to save hundreds of lessor flamingo chicks.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Community organisations, the SPCA in Kimberley, conservationists and private individuals are standing together to rescue more then 1000 lesser flamingo chicks are dying in the scorching heat just outside Kimberley. Volunteers from the community of Kimberley have been collecting newly hatched chicks from their abandoned nests and taking them to the local SPCA where they are hydrated, fed and looked after a local vet. Some 900 chicks were flown to Wonderboom Airport where they are being taken care of by Mike Bolhuis on his private property. The rest of the chicks are said to go to various wildlife rehabilitation centres across the country. Experts say if the rain stays away the pan could be completely dry within 2 to 4 weeks, forcing the adult flamingoes to move away.
metadata.Summary: The Kamfers Dam outside Kimberley is drying up fast. It is home to approximately 60,000 lesser flamingoes and they have been breeding at the dam for about 30 years. The dam is one of only four breeding sites for the lesser flamingo in the world. But disaster has struck. A vast area where the flamingoes have nested has dried out completely, leaving nests exposed. During the hot days the flamingoes leave their nests to move to the the small area that still has water leaving the chicks and eggs exposed. Eggs are breeding out and the chicks are vulnerable. In some instances the chicks are so dehydrated from the heat that they are unable to hatch themselves. Now the community of Kimberley have come together and have collected about 3,000 chicks so far. They are being cared for at the Kimberley SPCA, and flown to various rehab centres across the country. So far, about 1,400 chicks are at Mike Bolhuis' farm just north of pretoria, where he has hired experts to help look after the chicks.
metadata.Further information: There are various factors contributing to the dramatic drop in water levels at Kamfers dam -- The biggest issue is the fact that the Homevale sewage treatment plant is not functional. The treatment facility is supposed to treat Kimberley and the surrounding township's effluent water, treat it and then release the treated water into Kamfers Dam. That water is then used by the local golf course and the local mine, Ekapa Minerals - the remaining water is then available to the flamingoes in the dam. However, there is virtually no water flowing into the dam from Homevale, because the plant is not functioning. Instead about 10 megalitres of raw effluent flows into a nearby wetland and veld on a daily basis. Locals say this is 90% of the problem. On top of that the mine is still pumping water from the dam - because they have to and have the licences to do so - and on top of it the area has had no rain for over a year. There is a lot of internal politics around Kamfers Dam. The property belongs to Herbert and Brenda Booth, thus it is not a formally protected conservancy, which make conservationists reluctant to get involved. Mike Bolhuis, the detective and philanthropist has made his property outside Pretoria available to rear and rehabilitate some 1,500 chicks rescued from the dried up pan. Ekapa Mining have made their private jet available to fly the rescued chicks all over the country. (including to Pretoria). The community of Kimberley have been amazing. At the local SPCA are about 100 cars parked, with hundreds of volunteers assisting to feed chicks, collect chicks from the dam. They're building temporary enclosures to keep the chicks safe. There are even two locals vets assisting with the weak and sick ones. The chicks are fed a special concoction, via syringe and it's amazing to see how quickly they grow and become strong. The question is what is to become of the flamingoes once they are grown-up. Will they be returned to Kamfers, or end up somewhere else. Mike Bolhuis is determined that his 1,500 chicks will be rehabilitated back to the wild. Additional controversy lies in the fact that: Some conservationists are questioning the way in which this mass operation is handled. There are questions around Mike Bolhuis' permits and their legitimacy. And there are even allegations that Mike Bolhuis is involved in wildlife trafficking, and that the flamingoes are destined to end up at luxury estates in the Middle East. But, ignoring the politics, it is a story of people of all walks of life coming together and saving thousands of chicks that faced certain death.
